newsitem.title: USA: Local job mkt tight, not getting tighter--Minn Fed.
newsitem.headline: Local job mkt tight, not getting tighter--Minn Fed.

text.p: Labor markets in the ninth U.S. economic district have been tight with some scattered reports of wage pressures, but the local employment sector does not appear to be getting tighter, a Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis economist said.
"We do have tight labor markets ... and we do have reports of increasing wage pressures," Edward Lotterman, regional economist at the Minneapolis Fed, told Reuters.
He added, however, that "the labor tightness was worrisome last year but it doesn't seem to be getting worse ... nothing seems to be sort of in the offing that would cause alarm."

The Minneapolis Fed serves the nation's ninth economic district, which includes Minnesota, Montana, North Dakota, South Dakota, 26 counties in northwestern Wisconsin and the Uppper Peninsula of Michigan.

Lotterman said the tightness in the district's labor markets was spread through most employment categories. "It does cross many skill levels -- blue collar, white collar, college educated, non-college educated," he said.
The regional Fed economist also said the district's economy was still growing at a fairly strong pace. But he added that there are some indications that the speed of growth is slowing.
"(The local economy) has been growing fairly well for four years now ... (But) we see a few indications actually that the pace is a little slower than last year," he said.
Lotterman added, however, that the current business cycle has not faded yet.

"I think the economy will continue to be strong in 1997. We don't see things going into a recession here, but probably not large increases over 1996 ... So it's a continuation of that strength but not further acceleration," he added.

Lotterman said it was hard to get a precise gauge of consumer spending in the region. But he pointed out a few clues detected by the Minneapolis Fed, such as the spreading of discount stores and an increase in retail space.
"We had an increase in the square footage of retail space over the last six years that has been much larger than the increase in incomes," Lotterman said.
Meanwhile, the Minneapolis Fed economist said inflation remains mostly under control.
"In fact, looking at the CPI (consumer price index) for Minneapolis and St. Paul, it increased less in the last two years than the nation as a whole did," Lotterman said.
Lotterman also said the agricultural sector in the ninth economic district was expected to perform well this year. "On the whole, I think the outlook for agriculture is good this year," he said.

The Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis is headed by Gary Stern, who was the only member of the Federal Open Market Committee to vote against the maintenance of steady monetary policy in the latter half of last year.

The Fed kept rates steady until March 25 when it raised its target for the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 percent during the last meting of its policy-setting body. The minutes of that gathering will not be available until after the next FOMC meeting on May 20.
Stern is not scheduled to vote on FOMC policy actions in 1997 given the committee's rotation rules.
